## Daily closing levels for the 10-year JGB

The 10-year JGB yield closed at 2.05% on 17 September 2026, 2.14% on 18 September 2026 (+9 bp) and 2.19% on 22 September 2026, according to closing quotes published by the Japan Bond Trading Co. and cross-checked against data from the Ministry of Finance. The 18 September move represented the largest single-session increase in the benchmark tenor since the Bank of Japan exited its negative-rate policy in March 2024. Trading volumes on 18 September were reported at 2.4 trillion yen in the when-issued and on-the-run 10-year sector, compared with a 30-day average of 1.8 trillion yen. The 22 September close extended the rise, with the yield touching an intraday high of 2.21% before settling at 2.19%. No unscheduled operations were announced by the Bank of Japan on either date.

## Shorter maturities and the 2-year note

The 2-year yield rose 12 bp to 1.31% on 18 September 2026, according to data from the Japan Securities Dealers Association. That level was the highest for the 2-year tenor since July 2008. The 5-year yield closed at 1.72% on 18 September, up 10 bp from the prior session, while the 20-year yield closed at 2.58%, up 7 bp. The spread between the 2-year and 10-year yields narrowed to 83 bp on 18 September from 86 bp on 17 September. The Ministry of Finance's auction of 2-year notes on 17 September drew a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.12, compared with 3.45 at the previous auction in August. The next 2-year auction is scheduled for 15 October 2026.

## Bank of Japan operations and policy statements

The Bank of Japan conducted its regular outright purchase operations for 5-year to 10-year JGBs on 18 September 2026, offering to buy 600 billion yen at fixed-rate and variable-rate auctions. The operation was oversubscribed by a factor of 2.1. On 19 September 2026, the Bank of Japan released its quarterly outlook report, which stated that long-term interest rates would be allowed to "move more flexibly" in response to economic and price conditions. The report did not specify a target range for the 10-year yield. The next Monetary Policy Meeting is scheduled for 28-29 October 2026. Minutes from the September meeting, released on 25 September 2026, showed that seven members voted to raise the policy rate by 25 bp to 1.00%, while two members preferred to keep it at 0.75%.

## Domestic institutional flows and foreign activity

Japanese life insurers and pension funds reported net sales of 10-year JGBs totaling 1.2 trillion yen in the week ending 19 September 2026, according to weekly flow data from the Ministry of Finance. Foreign investors recorded net purchases of 480 billion yen in the same week, the third consecutive week of net buying. Regional banks reported net sales of 320 billion yen in the 5-year sector. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's JGB futures contract for December 2026 delivery settled at 146.32 on 22 September, down from 147.10 on 17 September. Open interest in the December contract stood at 112,000 lots on 22 September, compared with 108,000 lots on 17 September.

The Nikkei 225 index closed at 41,250 on 22 September 2026, down 0.8% from 17 September. The yen traded at 148.20 per dollar on 22 September, compared with 147.50 on 17 September. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's TOPIX bank index fell 1.2% over the same period. The Ministry of Finance is scheduled to auction 10-year JGBs on 1 October 2026 and 30-year JGBs on 8 October 2026. sources.title: Singapore Home Loans: The Silent Rate Sensitivity Killer
sources.body:
## The Great Singapore Sleepwalk

I have a confession: I love Singapore. The food, the efficiency, the way the MRT actually works. But the way this island treats home loans is a masterclass in collective denial. Everyone I know is fixated on the property price, the stamp duty, the renovation budget. Nobody talks about the interest rate. It is the elephant in the room, except the elephant is wearing a nice suit and quietly raising your monthly instalment while you admire the view from your 30th-floor condo.

Here is the thing. For years, rates were so low that a mortgage felt like a rounding error. You signed the papers, the banker smiled, and you went back to scrolling PropertyGuru. But rates do not stay low forever. They never do. And when they move, they move fast, like a taxi driver who just saw a green light. The problem is that Singapore's home loan market is structurally allergic to rate rises, and almost nobody is prepared.

## The Myth of the Fixed Rate

Let me be blunt: most "fixed rate" packages in Singapore are fixed for about as long as a New Year's resolution. Two years, maybe three, then you are dumped into a floating rate that tracks SORA or some bank's internal board rate, which is a polite way of saying "whatever we feel like." The banks know this. They price the fixed period as a loss leader, then make it back when you are too lazy or too busy to refinance.

And why would you refinance? Because the paperwork is a nightmare, the legal fees are annoying, and your existing bank will offer you a "loyalty" spread that is only slightly worse than a kick in the teeth. So you stay. You grumble. You pay. The bank sends you a mooncake every Chinese New Year and considers the relationship healthy.

I have friends who took out loans at rates that started with a one. They are now looking at rates that start with a three, and they are not happy. One of them, a smart guy who works in tech, told me he had "modelled it out." He modelled it out so well that he forgot to model the part where his monthly payment goes up by a few hundred dollars. Now he is cutting back on avocado toast, which is the Singaporean equivalent of a national crisis.

## The BoJ and the TSMC Effect

You might think this is a local problem. It is not. Singapore is a small, open economy, which is a fancy way of saying we get pushed around by everyone. The Bank of Japan, or BoJ, has been the world's favourite punching bag for decades, keeping rates low and exporting cheap money. When the BoJ even hints at normalising, global yields twitch. And when global yields twitch, Singapore's mortgage rates sneeze.

Then there is TSMC. Yes, the Taiwanese chip giant. Why does a semiconductor company matter for your HDB loan? Because TSMC is a bellwether for global demand, supply chains, and inflation. When TSMC sneezes, the world catches a cold, and central banks start thinking about tightening. That tightening filters through to Singapore's SORA, and suddenly your floating rate is not so friendly. I am not saying TSMC is deliberately sabotaging your mortgage. I am saying the world is connected, and your loan is not an island.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore does what it can, but it manages the exchange rate, not interest rates. So when the Fed hikes, we import the pain. When the BoJ moves, we import the confusion. And when TSMC has a bad quarter, we import the volatility. Your home loan is a tiny boat on a very big, very moody ocean.

## The Refinancing Trap

Here is where it gets truly sardonic. The government and the banks love to talk about financial literacy. They run campaigns. They publish guides. They tell you to "review your mortgage regularly." And then they make it as painful as possible to actually do it. The lock-in periods, the clawback clauses, the legal fees, the valuation fees, the fact that you have to take time off work to sit in a branch and listen to a relationship manager explain why their new package is actually a great deal.

I tried to refinance once. I spent three weeks gathering documents, only to be told that my loan-to-value ratio had crept up because the property next door sold for less than expected. The bank offered me a rate that was higher than my existing one, then acted like they were doing me a favour. I walked away. I am still walking.

The dirty secret is that the banks do not want you to refinance. They want you to stay put, pay the floating rate, and forget that you have options. The ones who do refinance are the ones who are already rich enough to have a personal banker who handles it for them. The rest of us are left to fend for ourselves, armed with a spreadsheet and a growing sense of resentment.

## What I Would Do

If I were in charge, which I am not, I would make mortgage contracts simpler. I would ban the phrase "board rate" and replace it with "we will charge you whatever we want." I would force banks to show you the total cost over the life of the loan, not just the teaser rate. And I would make refinancing as easy as ordering a Grab.

But I am not in charge. So here is my advice, for what it is worth. Do not assume rates will stay low. Do not assume your bank has your back. Do not assume that because you bought a property in Singapore, you are automatically safe. The market is not your friend. It is a casino, and the house always wins.

If you have a floating rate loan, stress-test it. Imagine your monthly payment going up by 50 percent. Can you still afford it? If not, fix it now, even if the fixed rate looks ugly. Ugly and predictable beats pretty and volatile. And if you are thinking of buying, factor in the rate rise that is almost certainly coming. The seller's agent will not mention it. The bank will not mention it. But it is there, lurking, like a durian on a hot day.

Singapore is a wonderful place to own a home. It is also a wonderful place to get quietly fleeced by a mortgage you did not read carefully enough. Do not be the person who finds out the hard way. The silent rate sensitivity killer is already in the room. You just have not noticed it yet.

spans.text: I have a confession: I love Singapore. The food, the efficiency, the way the MRT actually works. But the way this island treats home loans is a masterclass in collective denial. Everyone I know is fixated on the property price, the stamp duty, the renovation budget. Nobody talks about the interest rate. It is the elephant in the room, except the elephant is wearing a nice suit and quietly raising your monthly instalment while you admire the view from your 30th-floor condo.

Here is the thing. For years, rates were so low that a mortgage felt like a rounding error. You signed the papers, the banker smiled, and you went back to scrolling PropertyGuru. But rates do not stay low forever. They never do. And when they move, they move fast, like a taxi driver who just saw a green light. The problem is that Singapore's home loan market is structurally allergic to rate rises, and almost nobody is prepared.

Let me be blunt: most "fixed rate" packages in Singapore are fixed for about as long as a New Year's resolution. Two years, maybe three, then you are dumped into a floating rate that tracks SORA or some bank's internal board rate, which is a polite way of saying "whatever we feel like." The banks know this. They price the fixed period as a loss leader, then make it back when you are too lazy or too busy to refinance.

And why would you refinance? Because the paperwork is a nightmare, the legal fees are annoying, and your existing bank will offer you a "loyalty" spread that is only slightly worse than a kick in the teeth. So you stay. You grumble. You pay. The bank sends you a mooncake every Chinese New Year and considers the relationship healthy.

I have friends who took out loans at rates that started with a one. They are now looking at rates that start with a three, and they are not happy. One of them, a smart guy who works in tech, told me he had "modelled it out." He modelled it out so well that he forgot to model the part where his monthly payment goes up by a few hundred dollars. Now he is cutting back on avocado toast, which is the Singaporean equivalent of a national crisis.

You might think this is a local problem. It is not. Singapore is a small, open economy, which is a fancy way of saying we get pushed around by everyone. The Bank of Japan, or BoJ, has been the world's favourite punching bag for decades, keeping rates low and exporting cheap money. When the BoJ even hints at normalising, global yields twitch. And when global yields twitch, Singapore's mortgage rates sneeze.

Then there is TSMC. Yes, the Taiwanese chip giant. Why does a semiconductor company matter for your HDB loan? Because TSMC is a bellwether for global demand, supply chains, and inflation. When TSMC sneezes, the world catches a cold, and central banks start thinking about tightening. That tightening filters through to Singapore's SORA, and suddenly your floating rate is not so friendly. I am not saying TSMC is deliberately sabotaging your mortgage. I am saying the world is connected, and your loan is not an island.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore does what it can, but it manages the exchange rate, not interest rates. So when the Fed hikes, we import the pain. When the BoJ moves, we import the confusion. And when TSMC has a bad quarter, we import the volatility. Your home loan is a tiny boat on a very big, very moody ocean.

Here is where it gets truly sardonic. The government and the banks love to talk about financial literacy. They run campaigns. They publish guides. They tell you to "review your mortgage regularly." And then they make it as painful as possible to actually do it. The lock-in periods, the clawback clauses, the legal fees, the valuation fees, the fact that you have to take time off work to sit in a branch and listen to a relationship manager explain why their new package is actually a great deal.

I tried to refinance once. I spent three weeks gathering documents, only to be told that my loan-to-value ratio had crept up because the property next door sold for less than expected. The bank offered me a rate that was higher than my existing one, then acted like they were doing me a favour. I walked away. I am still walking.

The dirty secret is that the banks do not want you to refinance. They want you to stay put, pay the floating rate, and forget that you have options. The ones who do refinance are the ones who are already rich enough to have a personal banker who handles it for them. The rest of us are left to fend for ourselves, armed with a spreadsheet and a growing sense of resentment.

If I were in charge, which I am not, I would make mortgage contracts simpler. I would ban the phrase "board rate" and replace it with "we will charge you whatever we want."
